unitTitle: ISAs, Operating Systems, and Virtual Memory
overview: This unit compares x86, RISC-V, and ARM based on their registers (Register), calling conventions (Aufrufkonventionen), addressing modes (Adressierungsarten), and instruction formats (Befehlsformen). It explains how multi-user systems (Mehrbenutzersysteme) use privileged modes (privilegierte Modi), a scheduler (Scheduler), and interrupts (Unterbrechungen) to control program execution. Virtual memory (Virtueller Speicher), the MMU, page tables (Seitentabellen), and the TLB translate addresses and enforce access permissions; lazy allocation (Lazy Allocation) and paging (Paging) provide pages on demand or swap them out.

entries.short: x86 is a CISC ISA family (CISC-ISA-Familie) with complex instructions, variable instruction lengths, and multiple execution modes.
entries.explanation: x86 refers to a family of closely related but distinct ISAs. In the example shown, instructions are 1 to 7 bytes long; this variable length differs from the RISC-V instructions considered here, which are mostly 4 bytes long. The family supports legacy execution modes and is characterized by its accumulated complexity.
entries.example: An x86 instruction can be 1 byte or several bytes long in the examples shown.
pitfalls: x86 does not denote a single word size.
Variable instruction length says nothing about register width.
entries.heading: IA-32 und die x86-Familie

entries.short: IA-32 denotes the 32-bit ISA of the x86 family.
entries.explanation: IA-32 is the 32-bit variant of the x86 family, introduced with the Intel 80386 and continued in, among others, the 80486 and Pentium. It has eight general-purpose registers. In the calling convention described here, parameters are placed on the stack and the return value is in EAX.
entries.example: `cc -m32` selects 32-bit output for the program shown.
pitfalls: IA-32 is not the 64-bit extension x86_64.
A 32-bit ISA does not mean that every instruction is 32 bits long.
related: Registers and register views in x86
entries.heading: IA-32 und die x86-Familie

entries.short: x86_64, also known as Intel 64, is the 64-bit extension of the x86 family, originally developed by AMD.
entries.explanation: x86_64 extends the x86 family to 64 bits and adds, among other things, registers R8 through R15. AMD originally developed the extension; Intel calls its compatible implementation Intel 64. New word sizes were introduced through new execution modes, while older modes continued to be supported.
entries.example: RAX is the 64-bit view of the register whose 32-bit view is called EAX.
pitfalls: Intel 64 is not the original source of the 64-bit x86 extension.
x86_64 and IA-32 denote different word sizes within the x86 family.
related: Registers and register views in x86
entries.heading: IA-32 und die x86-Familie

entries.short: ISA extensions add instructions or capabilities to a processor family.
entries.explanation: VMX supports virtual machines, F16C converts half-precision floating-point values, and Transactional Memory supports speculative execution related to atomic accesses. An extension adds specific features to the existing ISA. Whether it is available depends on the processor in question.
entries.example: VMX provides features that support virtual machines.
pitfalls: An extension is not automatically available in every x86 processor.
Here, F16C refers to conversion instructions.
entries.heading: Genannte Erweiterungen von IA-32 / x86

entries.term: Registers and register views in x86
entries.short: Several x86 register names denote views of different widths onto the same register region.
entries.explanation: RAX denotes the 64-bit view, EAX the 32-bit view, AX the 16-bit view, and AH and AL each denote an 8-bit subview. IA-32 has eight general-purpose registers; x86_64 adds R8 through R15, giving it 16. ESP/RSP is the Stack Pointer, and EBP/RBP serves as the Base Pointer in the stack frame shown.
entries.example: EAX is the 32-bit view of the register region denoted by RAX.
pitfalls: These names do not denote four independent registers.
The stated register roles depend on the ISA and calling convention.
entries.heading: Register und Teilsichten

entries.short: A calling convention specifies where parameters and return values are placed and which registers a subroutine must preserve.
entries.explanation: In the IA-32 convention shown, parameters are placed on the stack, the return value is in EAX, and the caller removes the parameters after the return. In the x86_64 convention described in the notes, the first six parameters are placed in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, and R9, with further parameters on the stack; the return value is in RAX. RBX, RBP, RSP, and R12 through R15 are listed as callee-saved. The notes do not specify an ABI or operating system, so these details apply to the examples described and not to all x86_64 environments.
entries.example: In an x86_64 call with seven integer parameters, six are placed in the registers listed and the seventh on the stack.
pitfalls: The register order is not the same in every x86_64 environment.
Callee-saved means that the called subroutine restores a changed register value if necessary.
related: Registers and register views in x86
Return address in x86 and RISC-V
entries.heading: Aufrufkonventionen

entries.term: Return address in x86 and RISC-V
entries.short: IA-32 places the return address on the stack when calling a subroutine, whereas RISC-V typically stores it in ra.
entries.explanation: In IA-32, `call` places the address of the next instruction on the stack. In RISC-V, `jal` stores the return address in the specified destination register, usually `ra`. The return address identifies the instruction position where execution resumes after the subroutine.
entries.example: A typical RISC-V call using `jal ra, ziel` writes the address after the call to `ra`.
pitfalls: `call` and `jal` use different locations to store the return address.
The return address is not a function's return value.
entries.heading: Aufrufkonventionen

entries.short: A C program can be compiled into an IA-32 binary and displayed as assembly code with `objdump`.
entries.explanation: The compiler produces 32-bit output with `-m32`; `-O0` selects the unoptimized variant shown. The program can then be run and displayed in a disassembly using Intel syntax with `objdump -M intel -d`. The output recorded for the `count.c` example shown is 45.
entries.example:
```bash
cc -m32 count.c -O0 -o count
./count
objdump -M intel -d count
```
pitfalls: Disassembly shows machine instructions from the compiled program, not the original C source code.
`-m32` selects the target word size, and `-O0` selects the optimization level.
entries.heading: Beispielprogramm übersetzen und ansehen

entries.term: Differences between x86 and RISC-V assembly code
entries.short: The x86 instructions shown can use a destination as both a source and a memory operand, whereas RISC-V typically performs arithmetic operations on registers.
entries.explanation: In an x86 two-operand operation such as `add edx, eax`, the destination is also a source: the old value of EDX is added to EAX, and the result overwrites EDX. x86 can also perform arithmetic directly on a memory operand. RISC-V typically uses `lw`, `add`, and `sw` for this, since arithmetic instructions use register operands. x86 can set flags with `cmp` and then branch with `jne`; RISC-V can combine comparison and branch, for example in `bne`.
entries.example:
```asm
# x86
add DWORD PTR [ebp-0x10], eax

# RISC-V: sinngemäß
lw t0, 0(sp)
add t0, t0, a0
sw t0, 0(sp)
```
pitfalls: An x86 memory operand does not mean that an instruction can have any number of operands in memory.
The flags set by `cmp` are part of the x86 execution sequence.
entries.heading: Unterschiede im Assemblercode

entries.short: The optimization level affects whether the compiler shown keeps variables in memory or in registers.
entries.explanation: In the `-O0` excerpt, the loop variable and sum are accessed through memory relative to EBP. In the `-O2` excerpt shown, they remain in registers; `xor eax, eax` sets a register to zero, and `test edi, edi` checks a value without changing it. The sum is in EDX, the register for the third parameter of `printf` in the x86_64 convention shown. The excerpts use different loop bounds, so this difference cannot be attributed to the optimization level alone.
entries.example: `xor eax, eax` sets EAX to 0 by applying bitwise exclusive OR to the register and itself.
pitfalls: A register allocation in an optimized example is not a fixed rule for all programs.
The different loop bounds are not automatically a consequence of `-O0` versus `-O2`.
related: Registers and register views in x86
Differences between x86 and RISC-V assembly code
entries.heading: Die gezeigten Beispiele mit -O0 und -O2

entries.short: An addressing mode specifies how an instruction expresses its operands and, where applicable, calculates a memory address.
entries.explanation: With immediate addressing, a constant appears in the instruction; with register addressing, the operand is in a named register. With direct addressing, the memory address appears in the instruction; with register-indirect addressing, it is in a register. Displacement or base-relative addressing adds an offset to a register; scaled indexing adds an index multiplied by the operand length to a base. RISC-V supports immediate and register operands as well as memory accesses using a register plus an offset; scaled indexing is not available by default.
entries.example: `lw a0, 8(a1)` loads from address `a1 + 8` in RISC-V.
pitfalls: With register-indirect addressing, the register contains the address, not necessarily the value being loaded.
The 12-bit immediate and displacement fields shown do not apply to every constant in an ISA.
entries.heading: Adressierungsarten – Folien 15–23

entries.short: The effective address is the memory address calculated from the operands at runtime.
entries.explanation: With base-relative addressing, `EA = Registerinhalt + Offset`. With scaled indexing, `EA = Basis + Index · Operandenlänge`. This calculation enables, for example, access to an array element using its index.
entries.example: With base address 1000, index 3, and operand length 4 bytes, `EA = 1000 + 3 · 4 = 1012`.
pitfalls: The offset is added; it is not itself the effective address.
With scaled indexing, the distance between elements depends on their operand length.
entries.heading: Adressierungsarten – Folien 15–23

entries.short: An addressing form describes how many operands an instruction names explicitly and where any other operands are located.
entries.explanation: In the 0-address form, operands are implicit on a stack; in the 1-address form, an accumulator is used implicitly. In the 2-address form, an operand is both destination and source, as in `add eax, z`. A 3-address register-register form names two sources and a separate destination; a 3-address memory-memory form processes the operands directly in memory. The register-register form fits RISC-V's load/store architecture.
entries.example: In a 3-address register-register form, `add x, y, z` means `x = y + z`.
pitfalls: The number in the name counts explicit address fields, not necessarily all implicit operands.
In the 2-address form, the destination overwrites one of its input values.
entries.heading: Adressformen – Folien 24–30

entries.short: With overlapping addressing, an instruction's destination is also one of its sources.
entries.explanation: This applies to the 2-address form: the instruction first reads the old destination value, processes it with another operand, and writes the result to that same destination. `add eax, z` performs `eax = eax + z`. The destination and one source share the same address field.
entries.example: `add edx, eax` reads EDX and EAX and overwrites EDX with their sum.
pitfalls: The result overwrites the old value in the destination register.
The term describes the destination-source relationship, not memory accesses in general.
related: Differences between x86 and RISC-V assembly code
entries.heading: Adressformen – Folien 24–30

entries.short: ARMv8 in its AArch64 form is ARM's first 64-bit ISA.
entries.explanation: ARM designs processor architectures and licenses them to partners that manufacture processors. AArch64 shares the RISC orientation, fixed 4-byte instructions, and load/store architecture of RISC-V. ARM also supports pre-decrement and post-increment, a barrel shifter, conditional execution, and flags. In the register convention described, x0 through x7 serve as argument registers, x0 also serves as the return register, x19 through x28 are callee-saved, x29 is the Frame Pointer, and x30 is the Link Register; w0 is the 32-bit view of x0.
entries.example: `stp x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!` stores two registers and updates the Stack Pointer using pre-decrement.
pitfalls: `xzr` and `sp` are special register names, not additional general-purpose registers beyond x0 through x30.
The register roles apply to the calling convention described.
entries.heading: ARM – Folien 31–38

entries.short: Time sharing divides processor time among programs by having the operating system save and switch between their states.
entries.explanation: When the operating system interrupts a running program, it saves the program's state, especially its registers, Stack Pointer, and Program Counter. The scheduler selects the next program; its saved state is then loaded, and execution resumes. This lets multiple programs take turns using a processor.
entries.example: After a timer interrupt, the scheduler can switch from program A to program B.
pitfalls: The interrupted program's state must be preserved so it can resume later.
The scheduler selects the next program; it does not translate memory addresses.
entries.heading: Mehrbenutzersysteme – Folien 39–47

entries.short: Privileged modes determine which instructions and resources a program may use.
entries.explanation: In user mode, privileged operations such as input/output or access to configuration registers are restricted. In system mode, the operating system can perform such operations and control interrupts. RISC-V distinguishes modes M (Machine), S (Supervisor), and U (User); a controlled return to a less privileged mode can use `mret` or `sret`.
entries.example: A user program requests an operating system function through a system call instead of directly changing a privileged configuration register.
pitfalls: A user program cannot grant itself system privileges with an ordinary jump.
RISC-V has modes M, S, and U; there are not just two modes.
entries.heading: Mehrbenutzersysteme – Folien 39–47

entries.short: An interrupt is an asynchronous interruption triggered by an external event.
entries.explanation: An interrupt is not directly tied to the instruction currently being executed; typical triggers include a timer, input/output, or a network event. The hardware typically checks the signal at the end of an instruction cycle. The operating system saves the required state, handles the event, and then resumes execution.
entries.example: A timer interrupt can give the scheduler an opportunity to switch to the next process.
pitfalls: An interrupt is asynchronous; an exception is synchronously associated with an executed instruction.
Maskable interrupts can be temporarily disabled.
entries.heading: Traps, Interrupts und Exceptions – Folien 48–58

entries.short: An exception is a synchronous interruption associated with the execution of a specific instruction.
entries.explanation: An exception can arise from an illegal instruction, a breakpoint, or an invalid memory access, for example. The operating system can terminate the process, emulate the operation, pass the case on, or resume execution after handling it. A system call is also deliberately raised as an exception.
entries.example: An access to an unmapped virtual page can trigger a page-fault exception.
pitfalls: A synchronous event is not the same as an external, asynchronous interrupt.
Whether division by zero raises an exception depends on the ISA.
entries.heading: Traps, Interrupts und Exceptions – Folien 48–58

entries.short: In RISC-V, a trap is a control transfer to a privileged handler caused by an interrupt or exception.
entries.explanation: A trap is a control transfer to a trap handler triggered by an interrupt or exception. The handler saves or uses the required execution state, handles the cause, and returns in a controlled manner. In other contexts, “trap” is sometimes used more narrowly for deliberately triggered synchronous events, so the ISA terminology should be observed.
entries.example: A page fault transfers control to the trap handler, which checks the cause and, if appropriate, loads a page.
pitfalls: Trap and interrupt are not interchangeable terms; in RISC-V, an interrupt is one possible cause of a trap.
A trap is not necessarily an error, since a system call can deliberately trigger one.
entries.heading: Traps, Interrupts und Exceptions – Folien 48–58

entries.short: A system call passes a controlled request from user mode to the operating system.
entries.explanation: In RISC-V, `ecall` triggers the privileged transition; the call number is usually in `a7` and parameters in `a0` through `a6`, while Linux uses `a0` through `a5` for this. The jump target comes from a privileged register, and the operating system can check parameters and permissions. This distinguishes a system call from an ordinary subroutine call with an arbitrarily chosen target.
entries.example:
1. Place the number in `a7` and parameters in `a0` through `a6`.
2. Execute `ecall`.
3. The handler checks the request, performs the function, and returns in a controlled manner.
pitfalls: `ecall` is not an ordinary call with an arbitrarily chosen target address.
The operating system can reject a request or report an error.
entries.heading: Traps, Interrupts und Exceptions – Folien 48–58

entries.short: The trap mode determines whether events jump to a shared handler address or to calculated interrupt addresses.
entries.explanation: In Direct mode (`MODE = 0`), events go to the base address `BASE`; the cause is stored separately in a register. In Vectored mode (`MODE = 1`), asynchronous interrupts jump to `BASE + 4 · cause`. Thus, different interrupt causes have different entry points.
entries.example: With `BASE = 0x1000` and `cause = 5`, the vectored entry address is `0x1014`.
pitfalls: The vector formula applies to interrupts in Vectored mode.
In Direct mode, no distinct offset encodes the cause.
entries.heading: Traps, Interrupts und Exceptions – Folien 48–58

entries.short: Virtual memory gives each process its own address space, which the MMU translates into physical addresses during memory accesses.
entries.explanation: The Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates virtual addresses into physical addresses during memory accesses. The operating system controls the mapping and can isolate processes and enforce access permissions. A process's virtual pages can map to physical frames in different locations in memory. By contrast, Min/Max registers provide only a coarse-grained protection region.
entries.example: Two processes can use the same virtual address while the MMU maps it to different physical frames.
pitfalls: A virtual address is not automatically the same as the physical address.
Page translation does not require a physically contiguous memory region.
related: Page number, offset, and physical frame
entries.heading: Virtueller Speicher – Folien 59–74

entries.term: Page number, offset, and physical frame
entries.short: A virtual address consists of a page number and an offset, which remains unchanged during translation.
entries.explanation: For a page size of 4 KiB, `4 KiB = 2^12 Byte`, so the offset is 12 bits. The virtual page number identifies the virtual page; a page table maps it to a physical page number or frame. The physical address is formed from the physical page number and the same offset.
entries.example: For virtual address `0x00403ABC`, the offset is `0xABC`; only the page number is translated.
pitfalls: The offset is not changed during a normal page translation.
A virtual page and a physical frame are different regions, even though they are the same size.
entries.heading: Virtueller Speicher – Folien 59–74

entries.short: A page table maps virtual pages to physical frames and stores validity and access permissions.
entries.explanation: An Sv32 page-table entry contains a physical page number as well as status and permission bits. `V` marks the entry as valid; `R`, `W`, and `X` permit reading, writing, and execution. `U` permits user-mode access, `G` marks a global mapping, `A` marks an access that has occurred, and `D` marks a write that has occurred. An invalid entry or an impermissible access causes an exception.
entries.example: A valid entry with `R=1`, `W=0`, and `X=0` permits reading, but neither writing nor execution.
pitfalls: A valid entry is not automatically permitted for every access type or privilege mode.
`A` and `D` describe access status; they are not read or write permissions.
entries.heading: Virtueller Speicher – Folien 59–74

entries.short: The X, W, and R bits encode, in that order, whether a page is executable, writable, and readable.
entries.explanation: The bit order is `X/W/R`: `001` means read only, `011` means read and write, `100` means execute only, `101` means read and execute, and `111` means read, write, and execute. The patterns `010` and `110` are reserved. `000` denotes not a leaf entry but a pointer to the next table level.
entries.example: The pattern `101` means `X=1`, `W=0`, `R=1`: reading and execution are permitted, but writing is not.
pitfalls: The bit order is X, W, R, not R, W, X.
In this context, `000` is a table pointer; `010` and `110` are reserved.
entries.heading: X/W/R-Kodierung

entries.short: The MMU decomposes a virtual address, checks the page-table entry, and uses it to form a physical address.
entries.explanation: Translation uses the page number and offset and checks validity and access permissions. If the entry is invalid, user-mode access is not permitted, or a write is directed to a read-only page, an exception is raised. If the checks succeed, the unchanged offset is appended to the physical page number.
entries.example:
1. Decompose the virtual address into a page number and offset.
2. Read the page-table base address from a privileged register and determine the corresponding entry.
3. Check validity as well as privilege and read/write/execute permissions.
4. If the checks succeed, combine the physical page number and unchanged offset to form the physical address.
pitfalls: A valid page mapping is not sufficient if the requested access type is forbidden.
A failed check causes an exception, not an arbitrary physical address.
related: Page number, offset, and physical frame
entries.heading: Übersetzungsvorgang – Folie 72

entries.short: Multilevel page tables create lower-level tables only for parts of the virtual address space that are actually used.
entries.explanation: A single-level Sv32 table requires `2^20` entries of 4 bytes each, or 4 MiB per process, even when many virtual regions are unused. Multilevel tables divide the virtual page number into indices and create lower-level tables as needed. Sv32 has two levels with a 10+10+12-bit split; Sv39 has three with a 9+9+9+12-bit split, Sv48 has four, and Sv57 has five. A leaf entry can map a large page directly; in Sv32, that is 4 MiB.
entries.example: If an entry at the first Sv32 level is invalid, a second table need not be provided for the corresponding address range.
pitfalls: More levels save table space for unused regions, but require multiple memory accesses during a page-table walk.
A leaf entry maps a page directly; a non-leaf entry points to another table level.
entries.heading: Warum mehrere Stufen?

entries.short: Sv32 divides a virtual address into two 10-bit table indices and a 12-bit offset.
entries.explanation: Sv32 uses two table levels: `VPN[1]` selects an entry in the first table, `VPN[0]` an entry in the second table, and the lower 12 bits form the offset. For `VA = 0x00403ABC`, the indices are 1 and 3, and the offset is `0xABC`. If the physical page number is `0x12345`, the physical address is `0x12345 · 0x1000 + 0xABC = 0x12345ABC`.
entries.example: `VPN[1]=1`, `VPN[0]=3`, `Offset=0xABC`; with physical page number `0x12345`, `PA=0x12345ABC`.
pitfalls: The two Sv32 indices are each 10 bits wide; the offset is 12 bits.
The virtual page number is translated, while the offset remains unchanged.
related: Page number, offset, and physical frame
entries.heading: Rechenbeispiel Sv32

entries.short: A TLB is a fast cache for recently used virtual-to-physical address translations.
entries.explanation: On a TLB hit, a stored translation can be reused instead of reading all page-table levels again. Without a TLB, an Sv39 translation requires three page-table accesses in addition to the actual data access. On a TLB miss, the translation is looked up in the page tables; an invalid entry or impermissible access can still cause an exception. Large pages can cover a larger memory region with a single TLB entry.
entries.example: A repeated access to the same virtual page can use the translation already stored in the TLB.
pitfalls: A TLB stores translations; it does not replace the page table as the authoritative mapping.
A TLB hit does not override access permissions.
entries.heading: TLB – Translation Look-Aside Buffer

entries.short: With lazy allocation, a physical frame is allocated only on the first access to a virtual page.
entries.explanation: The operating system initially reserves virtual address space without immediately mapping a physical frame. The first access to the page that has not yet been mapped triggers an exception. The handler finds a free frame, sets up the mapping, and then lets execution resume.
entries.example:
1. Provide a virtual memory region without physical frames.
2. Handle the exception raised on first access.
3. Allocate a frame and update the page-table entry.
pitfalls: With lazy allocation, the exception on first access can be expected behavior.
Virtual memory is reserved before the first access, but is not necessarily backed by physical memory yet.
entries.heading: Lazy Allocation

entries.short: In paging, a selected page is swapped out to secondary storage and read back in when accessed later.
entries.explanation: When no free physical frame is available, the operating system can select a little-used page, mark it as absent, and write it to secondary storage. The freed frame is assigned to a needed page. If a program later accesses the swapped-out page, an exception is raised; the operating system loads the page back and updates the page table. Paging makes main memory appear larger, but causes slow accesses.
entries.example:
1. Select a page B that has been unused for a long time and swap it out.
2. Assign its frame to a needed page A.
3. When B is accessed later, load the page back and update the mapping.
pitfalls: Swapping out a page is considerably slower than accessing main memory.
Selecting a page to swap out must take its possible later reuse into account.
entries.heading: Paging: Auslagern, wenn keine Kachel frei ist

entries.short: Pinned pages remain in physical memory and are not swapped out.
entries.explanation: The operating system pins pages when they must remain physically available while in use. Examples include memory regions for devices without an MMU, such as network cards or GPUs, as well as parts of the operating system such as page tables. Pinned pages are not available as candidates for ordinary paging.
entries.example: A page table can be pinned so that the operating system always finds it in main memory during address translation.
pitfalls: Pinned does not automatically mean that a page is accessible to user programs.
Pinning reduces the memory available for ordinary paging.
entries.heading: Paging: Auslagern, wenn keine Kachel frei ist

entries.short: Page-table permissions can be set deliberately so that certain accesses raise an exception.
entries.explanation: The operating system can revoke read, write, or execute permissions to catch unauthorized accesses. During debugging, this can help detect array overflows or underflows, for example. Protection bits can also be used for performance analysis, such as counting accesses.
entries.example: A read-only page can catch an attempted write and thereby expose a program error.
pitfalls: A protection fault indicates a forbidden access, but does not automatically identify its cause in the source code.
Access protection relies on the page permissions that have been set.
entries.heading: Zugriffsschutz gezielt nutzen

entries.short: In Little Endian, the least significant byte of a multibyte value is stored at the lowest memory address.
entries.explanation: Byte order determines how the bytes of a multibyte value are arranged in memory. In Little Endian, the byte containing the least significant bits comes first; in Big Endian, the most significant byte comes first. This order concerns how a value is represented in memory, not how a virtual address is divided into a page number and offset.
entries.example: The 32-bit value `0x12345678` is stored bytewise as `78 56 34 12` at increasing addresses in Little Endian.
pitfalls: Little Endian reverses the order of bytes, not the bit order within a byte.
Endianness and virtual page translation describe different aspects of a memory access.
